title: Target Sum
statement: You get a list of non-negative integers and a target. Put a plus or a minus sign in front of every number, then add them all up. Count how many different sign choices give exactly the target.

example.caption: With 1 and 1 and target 0, the choices +1-1 and -1+1 both total 0. Answer: 2.

output.label: dp[i][s] = sign choices for the first i numbers with total s

idea.sentence: Many sign choices end on the same running sum, so count them instead of listing them. dp[i][s] is how many ways the first i numbers total s. Each number sends every sum to s+x and to s-x.

jargon.plain: The total of the signed numbers chosen so far.
Sums can be negative, but array indexes cannot. Add a constant (here the total of all numbers) to every sum so that -total lands on column 0.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: the numbers, then the target, e.g. [1,1], 0

compare.unit: steps (rough; n·S for the table, 2^n for brute force)

rows.name: Brute force
rows.note: Recurse: plus or minus for each number.

rows.name: Table over sums (shown)
rows.note: (n+1) rows by (2S+1) columns. Each cell is touched a constant number of times.

rows.name: Map or one row
rows.note: Row i reads only row i-1. Keep a map from running sum to count and build a new map per number. Only reachable sums are stored.

rows.name: Subset-sum trick
rows.note: Choosing plus for a subset P gives sum(P) - (S - sum(P)). So count subsets that sum to (S + target) / 2.

fast.takeaway: Do not list sign choices. Many land on the same running sum, so keep one count per sum and add counts when two paths meet.

stages.title: Offset table
stages.note: Columns are sums from -total to total, shifted so they are valid indexes. Row 0: sum 0 in one way.

stages.title: Choose plus
stages.note: For each reachable sum s in the row above, add its count to s + x in this row.

stages.title: Choose minus
stages.note: Add the same counts to s - x. When two paths land on one sum, the counts add.

stages.title: Read the target
stages.note: Read the last row at the target. A target outside -total..total has no ways, so return 0.

edges.title: Zeros double the count
edges.why: A zero can take either sign and the total does not move, so each zero multiplies the count by 2. Eight zeros give 2^8.

edges.title: Target out of range
edges.why: No choice can exceed the total of all numbers. Check the range before indexing, or the index goes past the end.

edges.title: Negative target
edges.why: Only +2-3 gives -1. This is why sums need an offset: -1 would be an invalid index.

edges.title: One number
edges.why: The single number must carry a plus sign. A minus gives -1.

gotchas.text: Sums can be negative. Shift every sum by the total of all numbers so that column 0 is -total. Forgetting the offset is the usual crash.
Check |target| <= total before reading dp. A huge target would otherwise index far past the table.
Out-of-range array reads give undefined, and undefined + 1 is NaN. A bad offset does not throw. It quietly poisons the counts.
Out-of-range slice access panics. Allocate every row (make([]int, 2*total+1)). The counts can be large, so int (64-bit on most machines) is the safe type.

recap.key: dp[i][s] counts sign choices of the first i numbers that total s. Each number x sends s to s+x and s-x.
recap.complexity: Time O(n·S). Space O(n·S), or O(S) with a map or one row.
moves: For each number x: add every count to s+x and to s-x
Return dp[n][target], or 0 if out of range
